newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel defence chief sees Syrian talks soon.
newsitem.headline: Israel defence chief sees Syrian talks soon.

text.p: Israel's Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said in remarks broadcast on Friday that he expected Israelis and Syrians to meet in the next few months to revive their deadlocked peace talks.

"To the best of my understanding...around spring, after the U.S. administration is established, there will be a meeting in which we and the Syrians must look for ways to bridge some of the gaps," he said on Israel Radio.
On-again, off-again peace talks that began in 1991 have been stuck over the fate of the Golan Heights captured by Israel from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who was sworn in for a second term this week, has sought to resuscitate the negotiations.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in an interview with an Arabic-language Israeli newspaper published on Friday, appealed to Syrian President Hafez al-Assad to meet at the negotiating table.

"Since you're an Arab newspaper, I call on President Assad to sit together and renew the negotiations, for this is the only government capable of making peace," Netanyahu told the Kul al-Arab newspaper.
Netanyahu rejects Syria's demand that Israel return the heights, a strategic plateau towering over both countries.

Israel's handover to Palestinians of most of the West Bank town of Hebron last week has prompted renewed interest in long-stalled talks with Damascus. U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk appealed to Syria this week to use Hebron as a springboard to making peace with Israel.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Wednesday urged his Syrian counterpart Farouq al-Shara to meet and said he was exchanging messages with Damascus.
Mordechai, who was speaking on Thursday night, said he hoped to reach a dialogue with Syria that would reduce the threats and dangers -- even if it did not result in the peace Israel wanted.
Israel's previous Labour-led government, ousted by Netanyahu, broke off talks with Syria in March 1996 after Islamic suicide bombings in Israel killed 59 people.

Syria demands that Israel resume the talks from the point at which they were stopped, insisting that the previous Israeli government had approved the principle of full withdrawal from the Golan Heights.

But asked by Kul al-Arab whether he would resume negotiations from that point, Netanyahu said: "Our method of work is to implement written agreements. We cannot look into matters that might have been said or not."
